    tokens = list(prompt_tokens)
    output = []
    for _ in range(max_new_tokens):
        logits = model.forward(tokens)     # NOTE: always forwards the ORIGINAL tokens

        next_token = argmax(probs)

        output.append(next_token)

expl: The bug is that `next_token` is appended to `output` but never appended back to `tokens`, which is what gets fed into `model.forward()` on the next iteration. Since `tokens` is identical on every pass through the loop, and greedy decoding (`argmax`) is deterministic, the model computes the exact same logits and therefore picks the exact same token every single time -- the loop doesn't crash, but it produces a degenerate, repeated-token output instead of a coherent continuation. This is a very direct illustration of why autoregression matters mechanically, not just conceptually: forgetting to feed the model's own output back in as input isn't a cosmetic bug, it removes the entire mechanism that lets generation make forward progress at all.

The loop correctly appends each new token to `tokens`, but the call to `model.forward()` was passing `prompt_tokens` -- the original, never-updated prompt -- instead of `tokens`, the list that actually grows as generation proceeds. As a result, the model was being asked, over and over, 'what comes right after the original prompt,' with no awareness that it had already generated several tokens past that point -- so it kept regenerating whatever token it considered most probable immediately after the prompt, producing exactly the repetitive-loop symptom described. Swapping `prompt_tokens` for `tokens` in the `forward()` call restores the autoregressive property: each step now correctly conditions on the full sequence generated so far, not just the original input.
